title: Within the order
hookLine: Sikhs speak of hukam, the divine order, to live within rather than fight (Japji 1–2)

cards: Two people get caught in the same downpour. One stands under an awning, glaring at the sky, phone out, typing how unfair this is.
The other pulls up a hood and walks, and halfway home notices the gutters running like small rivers. Same rain. Same wet socks.
Something different in how they stand inside it. The Guru Granth Sahib opens with a long poem by Guru Nanak called the Japji, part of the Sikh morning prayers.
Near its start, Nanak asks a question, and answers it with one word.

teach.h: HOW DOES THE WALL OF FALSEHOOD FALL?
teach.b: First, the question. In the first stanza of the Japji, Nanak asks, in paraphrase: how can we become true, and how does the wall of falsehood come down? He's already set aside the easy answers.
Thinking it over won't do it. Keeping silent won't do it. Piling up what you want won't satisfy the hunger.
Then the answer: walk in the hukam, the order of the will, which is written along with you. Second, the word. Hukam means an order, a command.
But in the Japji it isn't a boss shouting instructions. It's the order everything is already moving inside.

teach.h: HUKAM: THE ORDER EVERYTHING MOVES IN.
teach.b: The second stanza spells it out: by the hukam bodies take shape; by the hukam some are high and some low; by the hukam pain and pleasure come. Then: everyone is within the hukam; no one is outside it.
Third, who argues. The stanza ends, in paraphrase: Nanak, whoever understands the hukam doesn't speak in haumai, in ego. That's the turn.
The pain is inside the order. What fights the order is the self that says this shouldn't be happening to me. Fourth, what it isn't.

teach.h: NOT LYING DOWN IN THE ROAD.
teach.b: Living within the hukam isn't lying down in the road.
Sikhs work, serve, and stand up for others, and they do it inside the order too. The rain doesn't change. The quarrel with it does.

how: Sikhs recite the Japji as part of their morning prayers, and they speak of living in the hukam, or in God's bhana, when they meet what they can't change.

o: a strict rule that only the faithful must obey
the order everything moves in; no one is outside it
a Punjabi word for the poem that opens the scripture

games.q: inside the hukam — tap the pairs.
p: what Nanak asks how to bring down
ego, which argues with the order

s: the Japji says thinking hard enough will make you true
the first stanza sets thinking aside; the answer is to walk in the hukam.
in the second stanza, pain and pleasure both come by the hukam
so do bodies, and high and low.
living within the hukam means doing nothing
Sikhs work, serve and stand up for others; what drops is the quarrel of the ego.

games.q: you're asking Nanak's question: how do I become true, and how does the wall of falsehood come down? what does the Japji answer?
o: think it through, over and over.
keep silent and sit very still.
walk in the hukam, the order of the will.
games.why: thinking and silence are both named and set aside in the first stanza. the answer is to walk in the order that is written along with you.

practice: Notice what's already happening without your permission, the breath, your heartbeat if you can find it, a sound outside, the air on your hands, and let each be there: this, too, is happening.
Then call up one thing today you've been fighting, a slow line, a printer that won't print, and picture yourself walking through it with the hood up instead of standing under the awning.

wordCard.voice: Hukam: Punjabi, an order or command. In the Japji, the divine order everything moves within; no one is outside it. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi in Gurmukhi script: order, command. in the Japji, the divine order no one is outside of.

carryVoice: Your line: no one is outside it. The week ran from Jacob's beautiful patience, Ayyub calling out, Arjuna's dropped bow, titikshasva, acchedya and a Guru's sweet will to the hukam. That's day seven hundred twenty-eight, and a week.
